lesson.title: Non-Literal & Reciprocal Reflexives
lesson.subtitle: irse ('to leave'), quedarse ('to stay'), and nos vemos ('we see each other')

hook.title: How 'Ir' ('To Go') Becomes 'Irse' ('To Leave / Head Out')!
hook.content: Look at the difference between ir ('to go [to a destination]': Voy a Madrid) and **irse** ('to leave / to head out from here'): **Me voy** ('I'm leaving / I'm off!'), **¿Ya te vas?** ('Are you leaving already?'), **¡Nos vamos!** ('We're leaving / Let's get out of here!')!

pattern.title: Reciprocal Plural: Nos Vemos, Nos Hablamos
pattern.content: With plural subjects (nosotros, ellos), nos and se can mean 'each other': Nos vemos el lunes ('We'll see each other on Monday'), Nos hablamos mañana ('We'll talk to each other tomorrow')!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.english: I go (requires a destination: Voy a casa)
I'm leaving / I'm off! (no destination needed)

exercises.target_answer: voy, me voy, ¿te vas?, nos vemos mañana, nos hablamos
exercises.meaning: I go (requires a destination: Voy a casa), I'm leaving / I'm off! (no destination needed), are you leaving? (tú), we see each other tomorrow, we talk to each other
exercises.explanation: Adding me/te/se/nos to ir shifts the focus from the destination ('go to') to the departure ('leave').

exercises.prompt: You are standing up from a café table to head home. What do you say for 'I'm leaving now'?
exercises.explanation: Me voy means 'I am leaving'; bare Voy requires a destination (Voy a casa).

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'We will see each other on Monday'
exercises.meaning: We'll see each other on Monday

exercises.idea: say that you are leaving today ('Me voy hoy')
cues: Myself + I go (= I'm leaving) → Me voy

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.meaning: We'll see each other on Friday
cues: Each other + we see: Nos vemos

summary.outcome: Use me voy / te vas / nos vamos for 'to leave' and nos vemos / nos hablamos for 'each other'.

use_example.german: Me voy ahora — ¡nos vemos el viernes!
use_example.english: I'm leaving now — see you on Friday!

summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([25] Gustar: The Inverted Liking): discover why 'I like coffee' in Spanish is literally 'The coffee pleases to me'!

ir.context_translation: I am going to go tomorrow.
ir.etymology_derivation: Latin īre ('to go', preserved in English exit 'go out' and transit 'go across')!

voy.context_translation: I am going to visit Madrid.
voy.etymology_derivation: Followed by a + infinitive, voy a expresses the near future.

me.etymology_derivation: Walks left of conjugated verbs or hooks onto infinitives.

se.english_meaning: himself, herself, yourself (usted), themselves; to him/her/them (before lo/la)
se.shift_rule: Reflexive AND the 'se lo' replacement for *le lo
se.context_translation: I tell it to him/her today.
se.etymology_derivation: Whenever le or les meets lo/la/los/las, Spanish softens the tongue-twister *le lo into se lo!

nos.english_meaning: us, to us, ourselves, each other

ver.context_translation: I am going to see it/him today.
ver.etymology_derivation: Pronouns can hook directly onto the tail of the infinitive: verlo ('to see it/him')!

hablar.english_meaning: to speak, to talk (hablo: I speak)
hablar.etymology_derivation: Latin fabulārī (to converse, tell stories — English fable and fabulous) shifted initial f- to silent h-: hablar!

mañana.context_translation: Tomorrow I am going to work.
mañana.etymology_derivation: As an adverb (mañana) it means 'tomorrow'; as a feminine noun (la mañana) it means 'the morning' (mañana por la mañana = 'tomorrow morning')!

hoy.etymology_derivation: Latin hodiē lost its middle d and became hoy (the exact cousin of the -hui in French aujourd'hui!).
